value: In the conditional, devoir means should rather than must
With a direct object noun, devoir expresses a debt rather than an obligation
In the passé composé, devoir + infinitive often means 'must have'

evidence.notes: Derived from the other meanings of devoir presented in the same chapter.

value: In the present tense, devoir expresses obligation rather than advice
The past conditional is used for advice about the past (should have)

evidence.notes: Both entries follow from the stated condition and the parallel obligation sense.

value: When both verbs share the same subject, an infinitive is used instead of que
With causative and perception verbs (faire, laisser, voir, entendre), an infinitive may be used even when the subjects differ

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated contrast; the causative/perception exception is standard grammar.

patches.entity_key: Direct object pronouns forms and placement
value: In the affirmative imperative the pronoun follows the verb with a hyphen, and me and te become moi and toi
In compound tenses the pronoun precedes the auxiliary, not the past participle
le, la, and l' can also be definite articles; only context distinguishes them

evidence.notes: First two entries come from the rule's transformations and compound-tense behaviour; the third is the stated trap.

patches.entity_key: Direct object pronouns in compound tenses
value: No agreement when the direct object follows the verb
Indirect object pronouns (lui, leur) do not trigger agreement

evidence.notes: First entry is the standard counterpart to the agreement rule; the second is the stated trap.

value: In the negative imperative the pronoun precedes the verb
me and te become moi and toi only in the affirmative imperative

evidence.notes: Both entries follow from the rule's affirmative/negative word orders and transformations.

patches.entity_key: Direct vs indirect speech time expressions
value: In indirect speech, aujourd'hui may become le jour même and demain becomes le lendemain
hier becomes la veille and avant-hier becomes l'avant-veille
Direct expressions may remain unchanged when the report is made on the same day

evidence.notes: First two entries come from the listed indirect expressions; the third is standard usage with medium confidence.

value: soi replaces lui, elle, eux, and elles when the subject is indefinite (on, chacun, tout le monde)
After à with a person, a disjunctive pronoun may replace the indirect pronoun lui or leur

evidence.notes: First entry is standard grammar; the second links to the companion rule on verbs taking à or de.

patches.entity_key: Disjunctive pronouns with verbs taking à/de + person
value: y and en are used when the object is a thing, not a person
With most verbs the indirect object pronoun lui or leur is used instead of a disjunctive pronoun

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated contrast; the second is the standard default for indirect objects.

value: dont replaces de + antecedent, so de is not repeated in the clause
dont is not used for a place or time relation, where où is used instead

evidence.notes: First entry follows from the dont construction; the second is standard grammar with medium confidence.
